claims.text: Pulumi components let you turn a group of resources into a reusable building block.
With Pulumi components, you can define a network, a database, or an application service once and share it across projects and teams.
People using a Pulumi component work with its inputs and outputs without needing to understand every resource inside it.
The legacy AWSX VPC component manages the VPC, subnets, route tables, and gateways behind a few lines of code.
Pulumi has a new component state migrations feature that lets you ship the upgrade path with the component itself.
A Pulumi component state migration translates the saved state of a component and its children before Pulumi works out which resources need to change.
Component authors can change the internal design of a Pulumi component and include the migration in the same release.
The Pulumi state migrations API is experimental and may change.
There is a component state migrations discussion at https://github.com/pulumi/pulumi/discussions/24799 where feedback can be shared.

The AWSX VPC example at https://github.com/pulumi/examples/tree/master/aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration follows a network as needs change over time, starting with v1, upgrading to v2, and later moving to v3.
The legacy `awsx.classic.ec2.Vpc` component creates a VPC with one isolated subnet, a route table and its association, and an internet gateway.
In the example, a security group sits outside the `awsx.classic.ec2.Vpc` component and refers to the VPC.
Without a migration that connects the old state to the new code, an upgrade could replace the VPC instead of keeping it.
Per AWS CloudFormation documentation, replacing an EC2 security group's VPC ID requires replacing the security group.
The AWSX VPC example does not create a database.
In a real application, changes to a network can cause downtime or require more resource replacements for a database using that network.
If a database has to be recreated, its replacement does not automatically contain the old data.
The modern `awsx.ec2.Vpc` component is the upgrade path from the legacy AWSX VPC component while keeping the existing network.
The third version of the example removes AWSX and declares the resources directly with `@pulumi/aws`.
In the third version of the example, Pulumi still manages the resources, but the code controls each resource instead of relying on the component to create it.
Across all three versions of the example, the AWS resource IDs stay the same.
Across all three versions of the example, the security group continues to use the same VPC.
In the example's resource trees, the `awsx:` entries are component records and the `aws:` entries represent the AWS resources that stay in place.

In v1 of the example, the resource tree is rooted at `awsx:x:ec2:Vpc "vpc"` containing `aws:ec2/vpc:Vpc "vpc"`, an `awsx:x:ec2:Subnet "vpc-isolated-0"` component with its subnet, route table, and route table association, and an `awsx:x:ec2:InternetGateway "vpc"` component with its internet gateway.

In v2 of the example, the resource tree is rooted at `awsx:ec2:Vpc "vpc"` containing `aws:ec2/vpc:Vpc "vpc"`, which directly contains a subnet named `vpc-isolated-1` with its route table and association, and an internet gateway.

In v3 of the example, the resource tree is rooted at `aws:ec2/vpc:Vpc "vpc"` containing a subnet named `vpc-isolated-1` with its route table and association, and an internet gateway, with no AWSX component wrappers.
Pulumi's state records both the physical resources and the components that group them.
Each Pulumi state record has a Pulumi name, called a URN.
Managed resources in Pulumi state also have an ID from the cloud provider, such as an AWS VPC ID.
The legacy AWSX component wraps the subnet and internet gateway in separate components.
Modern AWSX removes the subnet and internet gateway wrapper components and puts the managed resources under different parents.
In the example, the Pulumi name of the subnet changes from `vpc-isolated-0` to `vpc-isolated-1` when upgrading from legacy to modern AWSX.
Pulumi aliases handle changes to a resource's name, type, or parent when its saved state remains compatible.
The AWSX upgrade in this example needs to remove component wrappers and transfer references to the resources that take their place, beyond what aliases alone handle.
To move an existing network to modern AWSX, you register the new VPC component with an alias for the legacy component type and a migration callback through the `stateMigrations` option.
The `migrateClassicVpc` function comes from the example's migration file at https://github.com/pulumi/examples/blob/master/aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration/v2/migration.ts.
A Pulumi component state-migration alias lets Pulumi find the old component.
The migration callback receives the saved state of the old component, followed by the state of its children.
The migration callback copies the saved state records, changes their names and parents to match modern AWSX, and returns `newState` and `successors`.
The `newState` return value of a migration callback is the complete set of records that should replace the old component and its children.
The `successors` return value of a migration callback is a map from each old URN that disappears to the URN that takes its place.
The first checks in the migration callback make it safe to run again: if the state already uses modern AWSX or plain AWS resources, there is nothing to do.
In the migration callback, an unexpected component type raises an error instead of the callback guessing how to migrate it.
The `rename` helper in the migration example copies the saved record and changes its URN, type, and parent.
The `rename` helper preserves the AWS resource ID and the other saved fields.
In the example, the `rename` helper moves the subnet under the managed VPC.
The two subnet entries in `successors` let the Pulumi engine know that the old component wrapper and the managed subnet point to the same new subnet record.
Pulumi uses successor mappings to update dependencies and resource references elsewhere in the stack.
In the example, the security group lives outside the VPC component, but its reference to the VPC still needs to be valid after the migration.
The VPC successor mapping keeps the security group's VPC reference connected to the migrated VPC record, which retains the same AWS VPC ID.
The third version of the example declares the VPC, subnet, route table, association, and internet gateway directly with `@pulumi/aws`.
The second migration in the example changes who defines the VPC-related resources in the program, and configuration can then be adjusted in a separate update.

The second migration, at https://github.com/pulumi/examples/blob/master/aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration/v3/migration.ts, removes the AWSX VPC component record and moves the managed VPC into its place.
In the second migration, both the old component and its VPC child map to the new VPC record.
In the second migration, the VPC keeps its AWS ID, and the other resources remain beneath it.
The VPC registration in the third version keeps aliases for both previous component types and both migration callbacks.
Pulumi runs the state-migration callbacks in order, passing each result to the next callback.
A stack still using legacy AWSX can upgrade directly to the plain AWS version.
A stack already using modern AWSX skips the first migration.
Once both migrations have run, both callbacks return no result on later updates.
Keeping earlier migrations with the component means its users can skip versions without having to edit stack state by hand.
After a migration changes saved state, Pulumi compares the new program with that state and calls the provider for any remaining changes.
Keeping resource IDs does not mean every upgrade has an empty preview; the example can still show in-place updates for provider defaults and tags.
To try the example, you start with `v1` and follow its README, using the same stack, backend, project name, AWS region, and availability zone for each version.

Before each upgrade in the example, running `pulumi preview` should show the existing VPC, subnet, route table, association, internet gateway, and security group with no creates, deletes, or replacements.
`pulumi preview` evaluates the migration without saving it.
Running `pulumi up` saves the migrated state.
If you maintain a Pulumi component, you can register the migration inside its implementation and ship both together.
With component state migrations, users do not need to write the migration, attach the callback, or edit their stack state.
When users upgrade the component and run Pulumi, Pulumi runs the migration as part of the normal preview and update.
For an internal change that keeps the same component inputs and outputs, users can keep their existing component calls.
Users do not need to know which resources moved or how the saved state changed when a component ships a migration.
The component state migrations guide at /docs/iac/guides/building-extending/components/state-migrations/ covers the callback contract.
The VPC example at https://github.com/pulumi/examples/tree/master/aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration contains all three programs and the migration code shown in the post.
State migration callbacks run during previews and updates when prior state exists.
State migration callbacks must be idempotent.
State migration callbacks return no result when the state no longer needs migration.
State migration callbacks rewrite state without performing provider operations.
A component state migration is a pure function that transforms the saved state of a component and its children into the state expected by a new component version.
A component state migration callback returns the updated state records and successor mappings.
In a component state migration's successor mappings, each mapping connects an old URN omitted from the result to the URN of the returned resource that takes its place.
If no migration is needed, a component state migration callback returns no result.
A state migration callback that returns no result can remain attached when using update plans.
A state migration callback that returns no result can remain attached when using targeted updates.
The restrictions on state-changing results from a state migration callback do not require removing an already-applied migration.
